newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Energy Dept opposes House nuclear waste bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Energy Dept opposes House nuclear waste bill.

text.p: The Clinton administration Tuesday said it opposed the House version of a bill to put an interim storage dump for nuclear reactor waste in Nevada, while the Nuclear Regulatory Commission expressed some reservations about it.

The House Commerce Energy and Power subcommittee held its first hearing on legislation that the Senate passed earlier this month on a 65-34 vote, which was two votes short of number needed to override President Clinton's threatened veto.
"My legislation minimizes the threat of nuclear waste by placing it in a suitable location in the short-term," Rep. Fred Upton, a Michigan Republican who sponsored the House bill, said.

But Lake Barrett, the Energy Department's acting director of the Office of Civilian Radioactive Waste Management, said the bill was "fundamentally at odds with the administration's stated policy" that a decision on locating an interim dump should be based on an assessment of the viability of building a permanent dump in Nevada's Yucca Mountain.
That assessment on a plan to bury waste from commercial nuclear reactors in Yucca Mountain is scheduled to be finished late next year.
Under a 1982 law, the Energy Department is to start taking control of the spent fuel January 31, 1998, a deadline the administration has acknowledged it cannot meet.
Utilities, which have paid into a fund for a yet-to-be-built central dump, are storing the waste at some 80 sites across the country.

"Because there are advantages to centralized interim off-site storage, we believe that establishment of such a facility...could partially resolve one of the most vexing issues facing the nation," the NRC said in a statement.
But the agency said it took no position on where the temporary dump should be built, and said the bill set unrealistically tight deadlines for it to license the facility.

The NRC also complained that bill would require the Energy Department to start accepting waste at the temporary dump by January 31, 2000, while it would have to apply for a license for the permanent facility by December 31, 2002.

This "sets the programs on a collision course with respect to a need for resources if adequate funding is not provided for both of these fundamental elements" of the waste management system, the NRC said.
The NRC also said it did not object to the bill's standard for allowable radiation exposure, while the Nevada lawmakers said it was sharply higher than standards for other facilities.
